The 56th Plenary Meeting of the General Assembly is resumed. The General Assembly will continue its consideration of Agenda Item 111, entitled Report of the Secretary-General on the Work of the Organization. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Democratic Republic of Congo.

Thank you, Mr. President.

Thank you, Mr. President. I am delivering this statement on the priorities of the SG for 2025 on behalf of the Group of Francophone Ambassadors. I have the honor of delivering this statement on behalf of the Francophone Ambassadors Group. And I would like at the outset to thank you for presenting your priorities for 2025. And I assure you that the Francophone Ambassadors Group stands by your side to protect strong multilateralism and to guarantee coordinated international responses to the many challenges we are facing today. The activity report that you presented Secretary-General, sheds light on the major progress made over the past year, including the finalization and publication, which will take place in March, on the UN Strategy for Multilingualism— Multilateralism. And this document is one that the Group of Francophone Ambassadors has welcomed enthusiastically because it is a major step forward in our commitment to strengthening linguistic considerations in all aspects of the activities of the Secretariat. We laid out important milestones, but the next steps will be very important to implement the strategy laid out in this document. In the GA resolution on multilingualism adopted on September 6th, member states requested the Secretary-General to publish administrative and operational directives needed to implement the framework. Could you indicate to us which administrative operational directives necessary for the implementation of the framework will be published in 2025 in order to let the strategic vision take place? We've seen the SG working in 2024 to ensure that linguistic and cultural diversity become a fundamental principle of digital governance and AI. As well as protection of integrity of information, as well as peace efforts. Francophonie and the Francophone group can count on solid partnerships with the Department on Peacekeeping Operations, as well as DGC, the Office on Digital and Emerging Technologies, the Office of the Coordinator for Multilingualism, and other UN entities. And there still, however, are major consequences stemming from the liquidity crisis on multilingual functioning in the UN. The use of French and English, the working languages of the Secretariat, as well as promoting multilingualism, are key elements of multilateralism which would be effective and inclusive. And that is why we must protect those functions from the current liquidity crisis caused by the failure of certain member states to pay their contributions, but which are assisted by the contributions of other member states. What guidelines were given to secretariat entities to promote participation of full collection of resources in 2025? That is to say, to ensure that member states and their peoples can fully benefit. And lastly, as for linguistic services, these should be seen as essential services protected from budgetary cuts. Is that a potential solution for member states, and how should it be implemented? You can always count, Mr. Secretary-General, on the group of Francophone ambassadors to take part in collective efforts in order to promote multilingualism and to make the UN ever more effective and representative of the diversity of its member states and the peoples it reaches out to, as well as the environments in which it operates. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Costa Rica.

Mr. President, Costa Rica thanks the Secretary-General for the presentation of his report on the work of the organization. It's a document that we really value for its clarity and conciseness. We recognize how challenging it is to summarize in just 23 pages the vast work being done by the United Nations. As regards this report then, Costa Rica wishes to make the following 6 observations. Firstly, we underscore how important this debate is. This debate is the main mechanism for formal dialogue between 2 of the 6 main organs of this organization, the General Assembly as the most representative organ and the General Secretariat as its executive arm. However, we are surprised that the usual participation in this debate in previous years is far lower in comparison with debates related to the reports of the Security Council or the International Court of Justice, just to give you 2 examples. We're pleased to see that this trend is being reversed this year. Secondly, with regards to the periodicity of this report review exercise contained in Document A, It is pertinent to note that it is only now in January 2025 that we are reflecting on the activities carried out in 2023. It's in everyone's interest that this discussion be held earlier so that the Secretariat can receive feedback on its work from member states in a more timely manner. This will strengthen the relevance and the impact of this dialogue. Thirdly, as regards the substantive content of the report, we are concerned that during the year 2023, multiple crises such as armed conflict, poverty, inequality, human rights violations, and the effects of climate change worsened. On this last point, We observe that the record for the hottest year in 2023 has already been surpassed in 2024. This reflects a worrying trend, and the devastating impacts of this are already being experienced. Efforts to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals face serious challenges due to insufficient financing and a lack of political will. In addition, the principles of multilateralism and civic freedoms are increasingly under threat. Nevertheless, the report does show that it is possible to make progress, albeit at significant cost, including the tragic loss of UN personnel in conflict zones. And this compels us to strengthen our resolve to support the most vulnerable populations. Fourthly, we recognize the valuable work of the organization, which in 2023 provided life-saving assistance to hundreds of millions of people in crisis context and also responded effectively to major disasters and made progress in achieving the SDGs despite financial constraints. We also underscore environmental initiatives such as the promotion of fossil fuel reduction and the fight against plastic pollution. We also highlight efforts to fight against racism and to promote human rights, especially through the empowerment of women and girls and the promotion of constitutional reforms. Similarly, we emphasize the important work carried out to fight against disinformation and work carried out in favor of inclusive and equitable digital governance. All of this has been possible despite financial challenges and delays in contributions, which have made it more difficult for the organization to operate in a regular way. Fifth, we recognize that the work of the Secretariat is not immune from criticism, and it is clear that it can do more to live up to the complexity of the collective challenges UN 2.0, the organization must remain dynamic, prioritizing data, innovation, strategic foresight, and measurable results. And at the same time, we require streamlined collaboration to address global challenges effectively and transparently. The UN 2.0 really now is more urgent than ever. 6th, While we welcome the report's achievements in peace and security, particularly in terms of initiatives on cybersecurity and arms control, we should not be afraid to acknowledge that global military expenditure has reached historic levels, and this at a time when billions of people face daily threats that threaten their lives, livelihoods, and dignity. The contradiction between The exponential increase in military spending, in contrast to minimal investment in preventing violence and conflict, the failure to meet funding targets to address climate change, and the lack of resources to meet the Sustainable Development Goals and to fulfill human rights is not only irresponsible, but it is also immoral. It's a matter of political will, and that is why We are looking forward to the analysis on the impact of the global increase in military spending on the achievement of the SDGs, as called for in Action 13 of the Pact for the Future. By way of conclusion, my delegation wishes to underscore the importance of moving away from working in silos, both within the UN system and among states as well. Only by working in a comprehensive manner, tying the threads between all processes and priorities, will we be able to maximize our efforts and achieve the SDGs. Looking ahead to the year 2025 and in relation to the major UN summits and conferences, we sincerely hope that 2025 will be an historic year for ocean action and climate action, for gender equity and women's empowerment, for the achievement of reforms and access to sustainable financing, and also for inclusive sustainable development that protects vulnerable populations and reduces the gaps that undermine human progress. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Costa Rica. Now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Indonesia.

Thank you, Mr. President, and I wish to thank the Secretary-General for his report and for outlining his priorities. Allow me to start by quoting the Secretary-General's report that the past year has tested humanity in every way. Indeed, the world is perhaps at the most challenging time since the founding of the United Nations. Humanity and international law are easily sidestepped by double standards. Geopolitical divides have taken over the work of this organization, and mistrust continues to fuel the flames of conflicts, preventing us from making progress in addressing climate change, poverty, and hunger. If we don't reverse direction, we risk stepping into a downward spiral leading to another League of Nations moment. Entering its 80th year, we must get the UN back on track. Multilateral reform is imperative and in fact is long overdue. The vision and commitments laid out by the Pact of the Future must be implemented. And in achieving this, I have 3 points to make. First, we need to recommit ourselves to uphold the Charter and international law, including to ensure full accountability of each nation on issues of international peace and security. We must build trust and avoid double standards in our action, and indeed direct our actions to contribute to maintaining and sustaining peace. Such principles must guide the Security Council reform, including the use of veto, the strengthening of the General Assembly and the ECOSOC, including strengthening the complementarity role of the GA when the Council is paralyzed, as well as this year's review of the peacebuilding architecture. Second, pursuing greater coherence between all UN bodies and within the UN itself is key to effective reform, and we therefore support the Secretary-General's approaches to create a more effective work of the organization, including the UN 2.0. And third, to put into action the principle of no one left behind. This requires fulfillment of existing commitments and ensuring mutual progress for all through the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities. The forthcoming FFD4 must succeed in closing SDG financing gap, including climate financing, and pave the way for IFA reform. Opportunities for sustainable growth must be available for all, including enabling digital transition, right to development, and downstream industries for the Global South. Mr. President, with a free and active foreign policy, Indonesia will always be on the side of hope, peace, trust, and progress. We will continue to work in earnest, leaving no stones unturned towards reforming the multilateral system and effective functioning of the UN. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Indonesia, and now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Zimbabwe.

Thank you.

Mr. President, we extend our appreciation to the Secretary-General for his report on the work of our United Nations, which highlights both our achievements and ongoing challenges. From conflicts to poverty, climate change, and threats to global peace and security, these are immediate issues affecting billions worldwide, and Zimbabwe stands ready to collaborate on addressing these priorities. The crises we face require more than words. They demand bold, decisive, and united action. To do that, multilateralism is crucial, and the UN must be revitalized to meet the needs of those it was created to serve. Solidarity should guide our responses to these shared challenges. As we approach the Peacebuilding Architecture Review, Zimbabwe remains committed to peacebuilding, recognizing its link to sustainable development and stability. President, turning to development, we emphasize the urgent need to accelerate Sustainable Development Goals and operationalize the SDG stimulus. Especially for the Global South. Climate change is an existential crisis, and we call on the global community to fulfill commitments to vulnerable nations. We advocate for reforming the international financial architecture to make it fair, inclusive, capable of supporting development around the world. In that regard, we look forward to contributing to the Financing for Development Conference, FFD4. Mr. President, to ensure that all countries operate on an equal footing, we reiterate our call for the comprehensive and complete removal of unilateral coercive measures, measures that have undermined the socio-economic well-being of affected nations including Zimbabwe. Their removal is crucial to upholding international law and fostering principles of solidarity and cooperation. In conclusion, Zimbabwe reaffirms its full support for the work of the United Nations. Let us allow— not allow narrow interests to polarize this institution. As a nation that seeks friendship with all and enmity with none, Zimbabwe stands ready to engage constructively for the betterment of humanity. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Zimbabwe, and now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Cuba.

Thank you, Mr. Vice President. We thank the Secretary-General for presenting his report on the work of the organization. We regret that since the last time we took the floor on this item, the humanitarian situation in occupied Palestinian— the occupied Palestinian territory of the Gaza Strip continues to get worse. While we're meeting today in this hall, the genocide by Israel against the kindred Palestinian people is continuing, and it has already brought about the deaths of more than 45,000 people. It's necessary to recall the role of the United Nations in the maintenance of international peace and security. The United Nations must put an end to Israel's impunity. We reiterate our staunch condemnation of the murders of civilians, including women and children, and the destruction of homes, hospitals, and civilian infrastructure. Similarly, we regret the murders of humanitarian workers of the UN system, and it's regrettable what is laid out in the report on the number of deaths of UN personnel and registered humanitarian workers. This has reached the highest levels ever in the history of our organization. Mr. Vice President, It's also disheartening to see that at a time when there's only 5 years left until 2030, we're only on track for achieving 17% of the targets of the Sustainable Development Goals according to the SDGs Report 2024. On this, and although the period covered in this report does not contain any deadline for adoption, it is necessary to underscore that in the path for the future, It was agreed to make urgent progress on discussions on the proposed SDG stimulus of the Secretary-General. This initiative is fundamental to keep hold of any possibility, any realistic possibility of achieving the SDGs by 2030. Without immediate financial support for developing countries, we would be saying goodbye to any hope of achieving the 2030 Agenda. In this regard, developing countries remain the most affected by hunger, extreme poverty, debt, the negative impact of climate change, unilateral coercive measures, and the consequences of the current international economic and financial order, which is profoundly unfair and exclusive. During 2023, Cuba, in our presidency of the G77 in China, which is the largest and most diverse bloc in the multilateral realm, drove forward an agenda to make progress with common interests for the Global South, broadening cooperation and ensuring mutually beneficial relations with the rest of the world. Under a common premise of making progress in the achievement of the 2030 Agenda, we promoted the role of knowledge as a generator for science, technology, and innovation, which is required in order to achieve the sustainable development that our nations so aspire to. We underscore how urgent it is to reform the international financial architecture. The United Nations must play its rightful role in this regard, and that's why we are grateful that the Secretary-General has defined this issue as one of his main priorities. The international— the current international financial architecture perpetuates disparities and forces the Global South to shore up financial resources and get into debt in order to protect themselves from the instability that the system itself causes. We reiterate how important it is to fulfill the commitments in terms of ODA by developed countries, and it's necessary urgently also to achieve a comprehensive and lasting solution to the problems of external debt. Developing countries cannot make progress if we continue to suffer from debt. The 4th International Conference for Financing for Development will be an excellent opportunity to make headway here. Mr. Vice President, we fully agree with the United Nations commitment to promote and to protect all human rights for all people without any discrimination. With double standards here. No country is immune from challenges, and no model should be put as an example above all of the others. And it's essential for all countries to work within a framework of respect and cooperation, moving away from selective or punitive approaches that have altered, changed the true meaning of human rights. We regret the absence in the report of relevant issues such as the right to development and the negative impact of UCMs when it comes to achieving human rights. It's not possible to make progress in sustainable development and in the well-being of present and future generations without leaving anybody behind. Well, we see a continuation of these illegal measures being imposed against the Global South and where our inalienable right to development is being denied. Mr. Vice President, the decision announced yesterday by the government of the United States to exclude Cuba from the list of the State Department of countries that supposedly sponsor terrorism where we should have never been included in the first place, somewhat corrects aspects of a cruel and unfair policy. It puts an end to specific coercive measures that, alongside all of the others, are causing huge damage to the Cuban economy with severe effects on our population. Despite this being a limited measure, It is a step in the right direction and is in line with the staunch will of the government and people of Cuba who have made an emphatic and reiterated appeal, and also the reiterated appeals by many governments, especially in Latin America and the Caribbean, Cubans abroad, political, religious, and social organizations, and many different politicians in the United States and other countries. Are extraterritorial in nature and a violation of international law and the human rights of all Cuban people. Mr. Vice President, we reaffirm the value of the global strategy of the UN for counterterrorism and the absolute responsibility of states to implement it in a transparent manner. We support multilateral efforts to consolidate the central role of the UN General Assembly. In the implementation of said strategy. Similarly, we reiterate our support for the adoption of a general convention on international terrorism, which would include state terrorism and bridge some of the existing legal loopholes in the definition of terrorism. This is an imperative in order to bridge gaps and deficiencies in the current legal framework in force. Terrorism cannot be eradicated if we continue to see double standards, manipulation, political opportunism, and selectivity when dealing with this matter. Sir, the current international challenges compel us to strengthen multilateralism. In this regard, the United Nations General Assembly must occupy its rightful place as the main normative and representative organ of the United Nations, and the Security Council must halt its interference in issues that do not fall within its remit, especially when it comes to issues that come within the remit of this General Assembly. Similarly, we underscore the intergovernmental nature of this organization, and we reiterate how important it is to avoid any initiative that tries to disregard this or that would seek to change it. Mr. Vice President, I am wrapping up my statement now by extending my— the support of my country to your work to promote multilateralism, sustainable development, the defense of international law, and respect between nations. Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Cuba, and now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Kenya.

Distinguished colleagues, at the outset I would like to thank the Secretary-General for presenting the annual report on the work of organization and for highlighting the priorities for 2025. We commend his tireless efforts in proposing solutions to address the root causes of the conflicts, in building a more equal, resilient, just, and sustainable world based on the 2030 Agenda, and in tackling ongoing and emerging threats, including climate change and environmental degradation. I reaffirm our commitment to international law, the principles and provisions of the UN Charter, and express our full support for the organization's efforts to maintain international peace and security. The year 2024 was an eventful one, full of complex realities, and the United Nations was once again tested for its strength and efficiency. As President of the Kyrgyz Republic, His Excellency Sadr Japarov underlined in his statement last year at the UNGA General Debates, military spending and armed conflicts have devastating effects on many nations and exacerbate poverty as well as inequality. As well as we all agreed during the Summit of the Future last year, we need to invest in our future generations and in our collective fight against climate change now. One of the gravest challenges facing our planet is climate change, which worsens daily, affecting nearly every country and community. The accelerated melting of glaciers and dwindling water resources in mountain ecosystems are deeply alarming. These consequences threaten livelihoods, exacerbate poverty, damage infrastructure, and harm national economies. To this end, Kyrgyzstan proposes expanding a mechanism to swap external debt for climate and sustainable development projects, aiding developing and least developed countries in combating climate change. These proposals, aligned with the Secretary-General's urgent call to reform the global financial architecture, as well as call for a Sustainable Development Goal stimulus of $500 billion per year. In this context, I am pleased to announce Kyrgyzstan's proposal to establish a Conservation of Nature and Mountain Ecosystem Trust Fund aimed at mobilizing resources for biodiversity and climate resilience projects. It will be operationalized through the UN Multi-Partner Trust Fund, and we invite all partners to collaborate on this initiative to protect biodiversity and strengthen climate resilience. Ladies and gentlemen, as mentioned in the report of the Secretary-General, biodiversity loss continues to threaten the future of our planet. At the initiative of Kyrgyzstan last December, the General Assembly unanimously adopted the resolution proclaiming International Snow Leopard Day. This initiative was put forward on behalf of the 20 countries that are home of this rare predator. Which have joined forces to preserve the endangered snow leopard and will continue to attract the attention of the global community to the need to protect biodiversity and high mountain ecosystems. As a mountainous country, Kyrgyzstan has consistently drawn global attention to the challenges of sustainable development in mountain regions. With our leadership and broad international support, the 5 Years of Action for the Development of Mountain Regions 2023-2027 is now underway. I invite all states to actively participate in this initiative and to join us at the 2nd Global Mountain Summit, Bishkek+25, in 2027, where we will review the results of the 5-year action plan. We are confident that all these initiatives align with the Secretary-General's priorities for 2025, and we count on the support of UN member states. Distinguished colleagues, I also wish to bring to the attention of the General Assembly that my country, Kyrgyzstan, is among the small states that have yet to serve on the Security Council. In this regard, we put forward our candidacy for a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council for 27-28. We look forward to the support of the fellow member states in correcting this historical injustice and electing Kyrgyzstan as a non-permanent member of the United Nations Security Council on June 26th. And in conclusion, I would like to highlight that under the leadership of Secretary-General Mr. António Guterres and with the active support of member states, our organization will continue to effectively fulfill its function and assist countries in addressing pressing global issues. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Kyrgyzstan. And now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Timor-Leste.

Mr. President, thank you for giving me the floor. My delegation welcomes the report presented by the UNSG on the work of the UN to support Member States in driving the 2030 Agenda, advancing climate action, promoting gender equality, protecting human rights, advancing peace and security, coordinating humanitarian assistance, promoting justice and international law, furthering disarmament, increasing drug control, preventing crimes, combating international terrorism, and consolidating United Nations reform. The report showcases the Organization's dedication to supporting Member States in achieving the Sustainable Development Goals despite the numerous challenges and crises faced globally. Mr. President, it is impressive to see the concrete results achieved by the UN, including coordinating humanitarian response plans for 245 million people across 74 countries and delivering life-saving assistance to nearly 160 million people in urgent need. The launch of key environmental initiatives such as the Water Action Agenda The Global Framework on Chemicals also demonstrates the Organization's commitment to addressing pressing global issues. The report also underscores the importance of addressing inequality and poverty in low-income countries, which is essential for achieving the SDGs. The UN's efforts to promote justice and international law, further disarmament, increasing drug control, prevent crime, and combat international terrorism are also crucial in creating a more peaceful and secure world. We appreciate the Secretary-General's concern about the lack of sufficient investment and political will which has stalled the full implementation of the SDGs and the fight against climate change. It is crucial for governments, international organizations, and civil society to work together to address these challenges and ensure a better future for all. Overall, the report demonstrates the UN's unwavering commitment to creating a more just, equitable, and sustainable world. The United Nations Secretary-General and his team have indeed made tireless efforts to address the numerous challenges facing our world today. Their dedication to promoting peace, justice, and human rights is truly commendable. Mr. President, as we move forward, it is essential to acknowledge the pressing issues that require our attention. The world is indeed plagued by war and violent conflicts, which is why continued support to the UN's vital work is crucial. There are several key areas that demand our continued to continuing focus, including UN reform, revitalizing the UN to better address the complex challenges of the 21st century. Climate change, taking bold actions to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and mitigate the devastating impacts of climate change. Digital and knowledge divide, bridging the gap in access to technology, education, and information to ensure equal opportunity for all. Implementation of the Pact for the Future, working toward a more equitable and sustainable future for all, as outlined in the UN's 2030 Agenda. Achieving SDGs, accelerating process toward the Sustainable Development Goals, which are critical for ensuring a better life for all people. Addressing inequality and poverty, targeting the root causes of poverty and inequality, particularly in low-income countries, to create a more just and equitable world. We believe that by continuing to support the UN's efforts and working together, we can make meaningful progress in addressing these pressing global challenges. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Timor-Leste and now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Nepal.

Thank you, Mr. President.

Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the Least Developed Countries Group. At the outset, I would like to thank the Secretary-General for his comprehensive report on the work of the organization and for outlining his priorities for 2025. Mr. President, as we enter the final 5 years of the 2030 Agenda, the challenges facing LDCs have intensified, demanding urgent and The LDCs align themselves with the core focus areas identified by the Secretary-General and offer the following perspectives. First, to achieve the SDGs and implement the DPOA, LDCs require enhanced global support. We call on development partners to fulfill their commitment of 0.20% of GNI as ODA to LDCs.

Thank you.

With more than half of LDCs at high risk of or already in debt distress, and with the ratio of external debt services to exports rising to 25.4% in 2023 from 15.9% in 2022 in LDCs, we need comprehensive debt relief and restructuring. We urge the full implementation of duty-free, quota-free market access to LDC products and simplification of preferential rules of origin. As we approach the 4th International Conference on Financing for Development, LDCs emphasize the urgent need to reform the global financial architecture to enable LDCs to have the necessary means to invest in sustainable development. Implementation of the $500 billion annual SDG stimulus proposed by the Secretary-General is urgently needed. Second, the climate crisis remains an existential threat to LDCs. While we contribute the least to global emissions, we suffer the most severe impacts. We urgently call for robust emissions cuts to limit temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius in line with the Paris Agreement. Current projections of 2.5 degrees Celsius to 2.9 degrees Celsius warming this century are deeply alarming and not at all acceptable. LDCs urgently need scaled-up climate finance prioritizing adaptation. LDCs require at least $93.7 billion per year for adaptation alone by 2030. We also call for full and effective operationalization of the Loss and Damage Fund with dedicated windows for LDCs. Third, LDCs recognize the transformation— transformative potential of science, technology, and innovation, including artificial intelligence. We call for strengthened support for the Technology Bank for LDCs to enhance our scientific and technological capacities. We also underline the urgency of inclusive governance of AI through the proposed independent international scientific panel ensuring LDC representation and addressing our unique challenges and opportunities. Bridging the digital divide with universal affordable internet access in LDCs by 2030 needs urgent global attention. Fourth, we appreciate the Secretary-General's commitment to the Doha Programme of Action. To accelerate its implementation, we urge focus on its 5 key deliverables, namely a food stockpile holding mechanism, an online university, an international investment support center, crisis mitigation and resilience building mechanism, and sustainable graduation support facility. We deeply appreciate the Government of Qatar for its comprehensive support and invite all the development partners to also come forward. Fifth, as 14 LDCs are on the path to graduation, smooth transition support is crucial to ensure sustainable graduation. We need an incentives-based graduation with the assurance that the international support to graduated countries will continue to ensure that the graduation is sustainable and irreversible. Mr. President, the challenges are immense, but so are the opportunities. The potential of our youthful populations, our rich natural resources, and our determination to build sustainable, inclusive economies offer pathways to prosperity. With the right support and policy frameworks, LDCs can be engines of global growth and sustainability. LDCs' success in achieving the SDGs and implementing the DPOA will be a litmus test for the global commitment to leave no one behind. Mr. President, with the beginning of the year 2025, we are embarking on a new year with important multilateral processes and meetings filled with new expectations and hopes. We hope the pace towards mutual development goals will actually accelerate this year. The LDCs stand ready to work with all partners to translate our shared aspirations in tangible progress for our peoples and our planet. Let us work together to make 2025 a year of transformative action for LDCs and for all humanity. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Nepal, and now I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Pakistan.

Thank you, Mr. President.

Mr. President, we thank the Secretary-General for presenting his comprehensive report on the work of the organization and his detailed briefing. The report thoroughly outlines the work of the United Nations during last year. The world is confronted by a complex web of challenges necessitating our concerted efforts to preserve and sustain world order, peace, and development. We concur with the Secretary-General's observation that widening geopolitical divides and mistrust, and impunity enjoyed by the powerful, are primary causes of persistent conflicts, poverty, inequality, and other societal issues. The rise in human rights abuses, discrimination against minorities, Islamophobia, and hate speech is alarming. This demands determined action to prevent further escalation and collapse of the world order. This can be best achieved through adherence to the UN Charter's principles, especially non-use of force, non-acquisition of territory through use of force, and respect for the rights of peoples to self-determination of their sovereignty and territorial integrity. It also includes opposition to foreign occupation, intervention, and new arms race. These current challenges cannot be realized only through enhanced multilateral cooperation within the framework of the UN Charter. Mr. President, even as we face the possibility of greater turbulence in international relations, the adoption of the Pact of the Future provides the international community with a broad and comprehensive roadmap for collective actions that could enable us to preserve the multilateral order and respond to the multidimensional challenges of our times. The Group of 77 and China have underlined that the pressing goal of the Pact of the Future should be to accelerate achievement of the SDGs and Agenda 2030. It is critical to secure timely implementation of the actions set out in Chapter 1 and Chapter 2 to secure the realization of developmental goals, in particular actions in 4 critical areas: 1, development finance; 2, trade as engine of growth; 3, technology; 4, reform of the international financial system, offering equal and a development orientation of FIIs and MDBs. The actions for peace and security set out in Chapter 2 of the Pact are perforce more general and will need to be translated into specific and actionable provisions in relevant forums with the support of the Secretary-General. First among these is the pacific settlement of disputes. The Pact was unable to address the conflicts that are raging across the world— in Ukraine, Middle East, Africa, and elsewhere. The UN's viability will continue to be called into question unless we can halt these wars and find ways to build sustainable peace In particular, we must deplore suppression of the rights to self-determination of the people of Palestine and Jammu and Kashmir. Preventive diplomacy should be activated to avoid new conflicts and resolve festering and prolonged conflicts and disputes. More determined and systematic endeavors are needed to secure implementation of the resolutions and decisions of the Security Council and the General Assembly. The host of modalities provided in the UN Charter for peaceful settlement mediation, arbitration, good offices must optimally and boldly be utilized, including the UN organs as well as the Secretary-General's Office, to promote resolution of conflicts and disputes. A holistic approach to conflict prevention is needed. We support the Peacebuilding Commission's efforts in conflict resolution through development promotion. We acknowledge the role of the UN peace operation in assisting host countries in transition from conflict to peace. Pakistan will contribute to the renovation and reinforcement of all UN peacekeeping operations. Secondly, the international community must halt and reverse the new and ongoing global arms race. The accumulation of nuclear and conventional weapons by major global and regional powers are increasing the prospects of even wider and more destructive wars in various parts of the world, including in several sub-regions of Asia and the Pacific. It is essential to revive the consensus we achieved at the first special session of the disarmament to enhance general and complete disarmament, including nuclear disarmament. A nuclear war must not be fought, nor should it be provoked by aggression with conventional weapons. All states must be assured of equal security. Confidence-building measures should be promoted at the regional and global level. There is need for new norms and actions to address the threats posed by new weapons and new technologies, and cooperation in the peaceful uses of technologies must be equitable and non-discriminatory. Mr. President, third, global efforts to eradicate terrorism have not been successful. Terrorism is spreading from Middle East to Africa and Asia. We must address old and new forms of terrorism. The UN's counterterrorism architecture must be rationalized and made more objective equitable, and effective. The Global Counterterrorism Strategy reflects our commitment to combating terrorism in all its forms. However, a comprehensive approach addressing all 4 pillars is required for effective outcomes. We must focus on combating new and emerging forms of terrorism such as right-wing terrorism, cyberterrorism, misuse of dark web, cryptocurrencies, online terrorist recruitment, incitement to violence, propaganda and disinformation, through social media regulation. At the same time, terrorism must continue to be distinguished from legitimate struggles of self-determination and liberation from foreign occupation. Mr. President, there is a legitimate and growing demand for reform of the UN Security Council. We need a Council which is more representative, democratic, efficient, and accountable. Comprehensive reform reflecting the interests of all member states is essential. The intergovernmental negotiations process provides the best and only platform for reaching consensus. The model proposed by the UFC Group, which expands only the elected members in the Security Council, is most likely to gain the widest possible political acceptance. Mr. President, Pakistan commends the Secretary-General's report. We seek collaborative and collective decisions to enhance the shared goals of member states for development and durable peace.
